title: Commented analyses of two real-world studies
text:
In this web extra to the manuscript The Problem with Univariable Selection in Regression Modelling-and What To Do Instead (Ullmann et al. 2026), we present reproducible analyses of two real-world case studies. For each case study, we first apply modelling strategies appropriate to the respective research question. We then contrast these results with those obtained using a univariable selection strategy, illustrating the implications of data-driven variable selection based on univariable screening. The analyses are intended as exemplars rather than comprehensive analyses of the underlying studies. Applied studies may require additional modelling steps depending on the research question and context. For comprehensive results and the full analyses, we refer readers to the original publications.
All analyses, tables, and figures reported in this web extra can be reproduced by running the accompanying R code.

Clicking on Code allows the reader to view the R code needed to recreate the analysis.

title: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
This example is based on the study of Tong et al. (2010). Previous work suggested that gene expression of peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) differs between invasive and non-invasive breast cell lines. Therefore, Tong et al. investigated its prognostic relevance in breast cancer using a retrospective multicentre study. PMP22 gene expression and clinical variables were measured in primary breast tumors by real-time PCR. The aim was to evaluate the association between PMP22 and prognosis while accounting for established clinical predictors: nodal status, estrogen receptor status, tumour size, and tumour grade. The modelling objective was prediction.
The PMP22 data are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19632791 (Heinze and Tong 2026) and include a data dictionary.
The original publication reports 249 patients. However, the publicly available dataset contains 248 observations. Therefore, analyses are based on the available 248 patients.

Required packages are loaded and helper functions defined.

# helper: extract HR, 95% CI, p-value, n and number of events from a
# fitted Cox model, one row per coefficient; reused throughout the paper
extract_cox <- function(fit) {
  s <- summary(fit)
  data.frame(
    variable = rownames(s$coefficients),
    n        = fit$n,
    events   = s$nevent,
    HR       = s$coefficients[, "exp(coef)"],
    CI_low   = s$conf.int[, "lower .95"],
    CI_high  = s$conf.int[, "upper .95"],
    p        = s$coefficients[, "Pr(>|z|)"]
  )
}

1.2 Data dictionary
The analysis-ready data set (pmpdata) contains the following variables:

1.2.1 Outcome

days: Follow-up time (in days) from diagnosis to recurrence, death, or end of follow-up, whichever occurred first

rezs: Event indicator (1 = recurrence or death; 0 = censored or cancer-unrelated death)



1.2.2 Predictors

PMP22: Peripheral myelin protein 22 (0 = negative, 1 = positive)

pT: Tumour size (1 = pT1 <1 cm, 2 = pT2 2-5 cm, 3 = pT3 >5 cm or pT4)

pN: Nodal status (0 = pN0, 1 = pN1)

G: Tumour grade (1 = G1, 2 = G2, 3 = G3)

ER: Estrogen receptor status (0 = negative, 1 = positive)

Factor variables (with suffix _f) provide labelled versions for presentation.
The complete-case dataset (pmpdata_complete) excludes observations with missing values. Of the 248 patients, 208 are included in the complete-case analysis.

1.5 Main research question
The objective is to estimate the association between PMP22 and disease-free survival while adjusting for established clinical predictors. A multivariable Cox model is specified a priori. No data-driven variable selection is applied.






Additional information: model considerations





In applied analyses, key assumptions of the Cox model should be assessed, including proportional hazards and potential multicollinearity. Pre-specified interactions may be considered where clinically justified. If the proportional hazards assumption is violated (e.g., for ER), time-varying effects can be incorporated, for example, by modelling an interaction of ER with log(days).

2.1 Univariable screening
Each model is fitted on the subset of data available for that predictor. Consequently, sample size and number of events can vary across models. This is often not reported.


Code
vars <- c("PMP22", "pT", "pN", "G", "ER")

# fit one univariable Cox model per candidate predictor, each using whatever
# observations happen to be non-missing for that single variable
uni_fits <- lapply(vars, function(v) {
  coxph(as.formula(paste0("Surv(days, rezs) ~ ", v)), data = pmpdata, na.action = na.omit)
})
names(uni_fits) <- vars

uni_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(uni_fits, extract_cox))

uni_display <- uni_tab %>%
  transmute(
    Variable = variable,
    n = n,
    Events = events,
    HR = round(HR, 2),
    `p-value` = format.pval(p, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
  )

uni_display <- uni_tab %>%
  transmute(
    Variable = factor(variable, levels = vars),
    `n (events)` = paste0(n, " (", events, ")"),
    HR = round(HR, 2),
    `95% CI` = paste0("(", round(CI_low, 2), ", ", round(CI_high, 2), ")"),
    `p-value` = format.pval(p, digits = 3, eps = 0.001)
  ) %>%
  arrange(Variable)

alpha_screen <- 0.05

selected <- uni_tab$variable[uni_tab$p < alpha_screen]

Only nodal status (pN) and estrogen receptor status (ER) are selected by univariable screening. PMP22, the variable of primary interest, is excluded. This occurs because univariable associations do not account for confounding. The effect of PMP22 (PMP22) is masked by its correlation with ER status (ER), which becomes apparent only after adjustment.

Additional information: interpretation after selection





Estimates from a model derived via variable selection are typically reported as if the selected variables had been pre-specified. However, standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values do not account for the selection process and are therefore biased, i.e., typically they are too optimistic. In practice, this limitation is often not acknowledged and the application of univariable screening is sometimes not reported.

title: A descriptive model for schoolchildren’s lung health
text:
We reanalyse data from a German study on the effects of ozone exposure on schoolchildren’s lung growth, conducted between 1996 and 1999 (Ihorst et al. 2004). Following Buchholz, Holländer, and Sauerbrei (2008), we consider a subset of 496 children with complete data on 24 variables potentially associated with the continuous outcome forced vital capacity in litres, measured in autumn 1997. The data are publicly available in the code supplement of Sauerbrei et al. (2014) (https://doi.org/10.1002/bimj.201300222).
Our goal was descriptive modelling. We aimed to identify the variables most strongly associated with forced vital capacity in a multivariable context, without necessarily implying that the identified associations are causal.
In this analysis, the pre-specified full model is contrasted with a multivariable model derived via univariable selection and a second multivariable model derived via backward elimination with AIC.

Required packages are loaded and helper functions defined.

# helper: extract point estimates, 95% Wald CIs and p-values from a fitted
# lm (or abe) model, one row per coefficient
extract_lm <- function(fit) {
  cf <- summary(fit)$coefficients
  data.frame(
    variable = rownames(cf),
    beta     = cf[, 1],
    CI_low   = cf[, 1] - qnorm(0.975) * cf[, 2],
    CI_high  = cf[, 1] + qnorm(0.975) * cf[, 2],
    p        = cf[, 4]
  )
}

Additional information: low prevalences





Such low prevalences give few informative observations for these covariates, which can make the corresponding coefficient estimates imprecise and unstable in the models that follow. In an applied analysis, this has to be accounted for, for example by:

Interpreting the estimated associations for rare covariates cautiously, emphasising the width of the confidence interval rather than the point estimate.
Checking, via leverage/influence diagnostics, whether the few observations in the rare category disproportionately drive the estimated association.
Combining a rare category with a conceptually related, more prevalent one, but only where this is clinically and scientifically sensible, not merely to increase cell counts.

This comparison is descriptive and post hoc, not a formal statistical test between models: apparent R^2 never decreases as covariates are added and so favours larger models regardless of whether the added covariates are truly relevant. Adjusted R^2 and AIC both penalise the number of parameters and thus give a fairer, if still informal, comparison of fit against parsimony across models of different size. For AIC, smaller values indicate the preferred trade-off between fit and complexity.
Although the model based on univariable selection includes fewer covariates, it explains only slightly less variance than the much larger full model. Apparent R^2 alone cannot distinguish a well-specified model from one that has excluded relevant covariates.
Although neither the full model nor the backward-elimination model can be assumed to represent the true data-generating process, this example illustrates why univariable screening can be problematic: marginal associations do not reliably determine which variables are relevant once covariates are considered jointly.







Key message



Marginal (univariable) associations do not reliably indicate which variables matter once other covariates are taken into account. Univariable selection excluded high_ozone and wheeze, both of which showed a clear association with FFVC in the full model (masking), while retaining variables such as age and birth_weight whose univariable associations were attenuated once correlated covariates such as height and weight were included in the model (amplification). Backward elimination with AIC, which considers all covariates jointly at every step, produced a model closer to the full model and did not exclude high_ozone or wheeze.









What would be done in a real analysis?



This worked example is simplified. A full best-practice analysis would additionally include:

Define the modelling objective (here: descriptive) before looking at the data, and decide a priori, based on subject-matter knowledge, which covariates define the starting set, the full model.
Decide whether data-driven variable selection is reasonable at all in the given setting, based on the modelling aim (e.g., descriptive vs. predictive) and on whether the sample size or events-per-variable ratio (model complexity) can support it.
Conduct a structured initial data analysis (IDA) before model specification, examining the distributions of the outcome and candidate covariates (e.g., outliers, implausible values, rare categories), missing-data patterns, and multicollinearity or redundancy among candidate covariates (e.g., via pairwise correlations), as outlined in Heinze et al. (2024).
Limit the complexity of the final model to what the available sample size can support, for example by applying sample-size or events-per-variable considerations for the number of candidate predictor parameters (Harrell Jr. (2015), Heinze, Wallisch, and Dunkler (2018), Riley et al. (2019), Ullmann et al. (2026)), to reduce the risk of overfitting.
Examine functional forms for the continuous covariates (age, birth weight, height, NO2, O3, temperature, weight) rather than assuming linearity, e.g., using fractional polynomials as implemented in the mfp2 package (Kipruto et al. 2025).
Consider relevant interactions where scientifically plausible.
Examine residual diagnostics (e.g., residuals-versus-fitted and QQ-plots) and influence diagnostics (e.g., Cook’s distance) for both the full model and the final selected model(s), to check the linear-model assumptions and to identify observations that unduly affect the results.
If a data-driven selection procedure is used, quantify selection instability, e.g., through bootstrap inclusion frequencies (available in the abe package) (Blagus et al. 2025).
Assess predictive performance using resampling that repeats the entire modelling process, including any variable-selection step, within each resample.
Report effect estimates with confidence intervals rather than relying on p-values alone.

title: A descriptive model for schoolchildren’s lung health
text:
We reanalyse data from a German study on the effects of ozone exposure on schoolchildren’s lung growth, conducted between 1996 and 1999 (Ihorst et al. 2004). Following Buchholz, Holländer, and Sauerbrei (2008), we consider a subset of 496 children with complete data on 24 variables potentially associated with the continuous outcome forced vital capacity in litres, measured in autumn 1997. The data are publicly available in the code supplement of Sauerbrei et al. (2014) (https://doi.org/10.1002/bimj.201300222).
Our goal was descriptive modelling. We aimed to identify the variables most strongly associated with forced vital capacity in a multivariable context, without necessarily implying that the identified associations are causal.
In this analysis, the pre-specified full model is contrasted with a multivariable model derived via univariable selection and a second multivariable model derived via backward elimination with AIC.

Several binary covariates are rare, with fewer than 10% of children affected: short_breath and wheeze (5.2% each), hay_fever (7.5%), and cough_exerc (6.7%). nr_med is similarly sparse (89.7% of children took no medication; only 4 took two or three).






Additional information: low prevalences





Such low prevalences give few informative observations for these covariates, which can make the corresponding coefficient estimates imprecise and unstable in the models that follow. In an applied analysis, this has to be accounted for, for example by:

Interpreting the estimated associations for rare covariates cautiously, emphasising the width of the confidence interval rather than the point estimate.
Checking, via leverage/influence diagnostics, whether the few observations in the rare category disproportionately drive the estimated association.
Combining a rare category with a conceptually related, more prevalent one, but only where this is clinically and scientifically sensible, not merely to increase cell counts.
Using estimation methods less sensitive to small cell counts (e.g., penalised/Firth-type regression, or bootstrap confidence intervals).
Reporting a sensitivity analysis that excludes rare covariates, to check whether conclusions for the remaining covariates depend on their inclusion.

This comparison is descriptive and post hoc, not a formal statistical test between models: apparent R^2 never decreases as covariates are added and so favours larger models regardless of whether the added covariates are truly relevant. Adjusted R^2 and AIC both penalise the number of parameters and thus give a fairer, if still informal, comparison of fit against parsimony across models of different size. For AIC, smaller values indicate the preferred trade-off between fit and complexity.
Although the model based on univariable selection includes fewer covariates, it explains only slightly less variance than the much larger full model. Apparent R^2 alone cannot distinguish a well-specified model from one that has excluded relevant covariates.
Although neither the full model nor the backward-elimination model can be assumed to represent the true data-generating process, this example illustrates why univariable screening can be problematic: marginal associations do not reliably determine which variables are relevant once covariates are considered jointly.







Key message



Marginal (univariable) associations do not reliably indicate which variables matter once other covariates are taken into account. Univariable selection excluded high_ozone and wheeze, both of which showed a clear association with FFVC in the full model (masking), while retaining variables such as age and birth_weight whose univariable associations were attenuated once correlated covariates such as height and weight were included in the model (amplification). Backward elimination with AIC, which considers all covariates jointly at every step, produced a model closer to the full model and did not exclude high_ozone or wheeze.









What would be done in a real analysis?



This worked example is simplified. A full best-practice analysis would additionally include:

Define the modelling objective (here: descriptive) before looking at the data, and decide a priori, based on subject-matter knowledge, which covariates define the starting set, the full model.
Decide whether data-driven variable selection is reasonable at all in the given setting, based on the modelling aim (e.g., descriptive vs. predictive) and on whether the sample size or events-per-variable ratio (model complexity) can support it.
Conduct a structured initial data analysis (IDA) before model specification, examining the distributions of the outcome and candidate covariates (e.g., outliers, implausible values, rare categories), missing-data patterns, and multicollinearity or redundancy among candidate covariates (e.g., via pairwise correlations), as outlined in Heinze et al. (2024).
Limit the complexity of the final model to what the available sample size can support, for example by applying sample-size or events-per-variable considerations for the number of candidate predictor parameters (Harrell Jr. (2015), Heinze, Wallisch, and Dunkler (2018), Riley et al. (2019), Ullmann et al. (2026)), to reduce the risk of overfitting.
Examine functional forms for the continuous covariates (age, birth weight, height, NO2, O3, temperature, weight) rather than assuming linearity, e.g., using fractional polynomials as implemented in the mfp2 package (Kipruto et al. 2025).
Consider relevant interactions where scientifically plausible.
Examine residual diagnostics (e.g., residuals-versus-fitted and QQ-plots) and influence diagnostics (e.g., Cook’s distance) for both the full model and the final selected model(s), to check the linear-model assumptions and to identify observations that unduly affect the results.
If a data-driven selection procedure is used, quantify selection instability, e.g., through bootstrap inclusion frequencies (available in the abe package) (Blagus et al. 2025).
Assess predictive performance using resampling that repeats the entire modelling process, including any variable-selection step, within each resample.
Report effect estimates with confidence intervals rather than relying on p-values alone.

title: Identifying biomarkers for cancer prognosis
text:
This example is based on the study of Tong et al. (2010). Previous work suggested that gene expression of peripheral myelin protein 22 (PMP22) differs between invasive and non-invasive breast cell lines. Therefore, Tong et al. investigated its prognostic relevance in breast cancer using a retrospective multicentre study. PMP22 gene expression and clinical variables were measured in primary breast tumors by real-time PCR. The aim was to evaluate the association between PMP22 and prognosis while accounting for established clinical predictors: nodal status, estrogen receptor status, tumour size, and tumour grade. The modelling objective was prediction.
The PMP22 data are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19632791 (Heinze and Tong 2026) and include a data dictionary.
The original publication reports 249 patients. However, the publicly available dataset contains 248 observations. Therefore, analyses are based on the available 248 patients.

# helper: extract HR, 95% CI, p-value, n and number of events from a
# fitted Cox model, one row per coefficient; reused throughout the paper
extract_cox <- function(fit) {
  s <- summary(fit)

    variable = rownames(s$coefficients),
    n        = fit$n,

    CI_low   = s$conf.int[, "lower .95"],
    CI_high  = s$conf.int[, "upper .95"],

1.2 Data dictionary
The analysis-ready data set (pmpdata) contains the following variables:

1.2.1 Outcome

A tabular presentation in a publication could have the following form. (In practice, the sample sizes and number of events used in the different models are typically not shown.)

  transmute(

    `n (events)_uni` = paste0(n, " (", events, ")"),
    HR_uni = round(HR, 2),
    CI_uni = paste0("(", round(CI_low, 2), ", ", round(CI_high, 2), ")"),

Additional information: interpretation after selection





Estimates from a model derived via variable selection are typically reported as if the selected variables had been pre-specified. However, standard errors, confidence intervals, and p-values do not account for the selection process and are therefore biased, i.e., typically they are too optimistic. In practice, this limitation is often not acknowledged and the application of univariable screening is sometimes not reported.
